subtopic: MR. VALADE-ALLEGED WRONGFUL POSSESSION OF LETTER BY MEMBER FOR SHERBROOKE
MR. VALADE-ALLEGED WRONGFUL POSSESSION OF LETTER BY MEMBER FOR SHERBROOKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning the general behaviour of members of parliament as far as the provisions of the Post Office Act are concerned and I am doing so in order that the public may continue to have the confidence it should have in the Canadian postal service. I should like to refer to the Post Office Act, Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, vol. 4, chapter 212, and more particularly to section 39 which reads as follows:
Subject to the provisions of this act and the regulations respecting undeliverable mail, mailable matter becomes the property of the person to whom it is addressed when it is deposited in a post office.
I also wish to refer to the provisions of section 55 which read as follows:
Every person who unlawfully opens or wilfully keeps, secretes, delays or detains, or procures, or suffers to be unlawfully opened, kept, secreted, or detained, any mail bag. post letters, or other article of mail, or any receptacle authorized by the Postmaster General for the deposit of mail, whether the same came into the possession of the offender by finding or otherwise, is guilty of an indictable offence.
In order to elaborate further my question of privilege, I should like to quote section 73 (1) dealing with penalties:
Every person who is guilty of an indictable offence under this act is liable, on conviction, to a fine not exceeding three thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or to both fine and imprisonment.
Subsection (2) reads as follows:
Every person who is guilty of an offence under this act, other than an indictable offence, is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two months or to both fine and imprisonment.
I have here an affidavit relating to the above sections which I have just read and,
with the consent of the house, I would like to table this affidavit.
It reads as follows:
Sherbrooke, October 13, 1964.
I Robert Delisle, a student at Sherbrooke university, after having been sworn on the Holy Gospel, declare and say:
1.	-I have taken note in Hansard of October 8, 1964, of Mr. Gerard Chapdelaine's question of privilege.
2.	In that question of privilege, the member of parliament for Sherbrooke mentions a letter which was sent to me by Mr. Maurice Allard, secretary of Hon. Leon Baleer.
3 I admit I won the Molson trophy at a golf tournament at Sherbrooke university.
4.	I never gave to Mr. Chapdelaine the letter Mr. Allard wrote to me.
5.	I never received the said letter and it was never given to me by anybody.
6.	I conclude that the said letter was intercepted for reasons I am personally unaware of.
7.	As a Canadian citizen, I want to receive the letters addressed to me.
In witness whereof, I have read this document and signed
Robert Delisle.
Sworn before me at Sherbrooke, this 13th day of October, 1964.
Louise Bruneau, C.S.C.
St-Frangois district
Now, Mr. Speaker, on October 8 last the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) raised in this house a question of privilege concerning the same Robert Delisle, a student at Sherbrooke university, in relation to a letter he never received, according to his affidavit, and which is in the hands of the hon. member for Sherbrooke, as he stated in this house on October 8, 1964, and as reported in the left hand column of page 8864 of Hansard.
In the circumstances I ask the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) to order an investigation into this matter and to make the result known to the house as soon as possible.
Besides, I have also in hand page 8864 of Hansard for October 8, 1964, reporting the statement of the hon. member for Sherbrooke as follows:
I am ready to table this letter so that all the hon. members might see it.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Postmaster General to order an investigation and to report to the house on the next occasion.

subtopic: EXPERIMENTAL SPRAYING FOR SPRUCE BUDWORM CONTROL
EXPERIMENTAL SPRAYING FOR SPRUCE BUDWORM CONTROL
speechtext:
1.	What was the role of the federal government in the experimental spraying of 160,000 acres in New Brunswick with phosphamidon for spruce budworm control?
2.	Why was a much smaller area not chosen for experimental spraying?
Hon Maurice Sauve (Minister of Forestry):
1. The spraying of 160,000 acres in New Brunswick with phosphamidon in 1964 was carried out as part of the provincial opera-
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
tional program of Forest Protection Limited, the crown company charged with control operations against the spruce budworm in that province. Their decision to employ phosphamidon on an operational scale was reviewed and accepted by the interdepartmental committee on forest spraying in November 1963 with members representing fisheries interests expressing their strong desire to have phosphamidon used for the entire spray program for approximately 2.4 million acres because of its recognized low toxicity to fish. The 160,000 acres treated with phosphamidon were selected to include the major fish spawning streams within the spray program and to cover certain areas where a developing in-sistance of spruce budworm populations to D.D.T. was known to exist. Cost considerations prevented the broader use of this material which had been under study by the Department of Forestry for several years in its concerted search for alternative material to D.D.T. that would produce a desirable degree of budworm control with reduced effects on fish and also wildlife. Following laboratory toxicity trials against the budworm and fish in 1960 and 1961, experimental aerial applications were made in 1962 to several plots in New Brunswick involving about 600 acres of forest. The results were encouraging and prompted an operational test on about 40,000 acres in 1963. Again the results were satisfactory and formed the basis of the Department of Forestry's recommendation prior to the 1964 spray program that phosphamidon might be used with benefit on areas where the fish hazard was high or where budworm resistance to D.D.T. was apparent.
2. The area of 160,000 acres was decided upon by Forest Protection Limited as the minimum necessary to cover areas of high fish hazard and of developing budworm resistance to D.D.T.

speechtext:
I was asked two questions yester-
[Mr. Grafftey.l

day. Perhaps I might reply first to the question of the Leader of the Opposition, who inquired:
-whether it is a fact that the United States borrowed moneys from the international monetary fund within the last few days in order to lend Canada funds needed to repay the Canadian account with that fund.
The simple answer to this question would be no. However, I should like to reply more fully.
On September 30 I stated that the Canadian government had repaid a further $50 million U.S. to the international monetary fund, reducing to $57.2 million U.S. the remaining Canadian debt to the fund. The original borrowing in June, 1962 was for $300 million U.S.
On the same day the United States for its own purposes borrowed $100 million U.S. from the fund. The currencies borrowed by the United States included the equivalent of $25 million U.S. in Netherlands guilders and $25 million U.S. in Deutsche marks. Canada used its holdings of U.S. dollars to purchase these currencies from the United States, and used the currencies thus acquired to repay the fund.
I should like to explain briefly the reason for following this procedure. Canada holds most of its reserves in the form of U.S. dollars, but the fund cannot at the present time accept U.S. dollars in repayment of outstanding debts because the fund's holdings of U.S. dollars are in excess of 75 per cent of the United States quota. Therefore, to repay the fund, Canada had to use currencies other than U.S. dollars. We could obtain these currencies either by purchasing them in the open market or by purchasing them from the United States in the manner I have just described. The latter alternative was chosen because it provided more effective support to the United States balance of payments and this, of course, would not in any way increase the cost to us.

These arrangements were made before the British election, and no new arrangements have been entered into since. Some use was made by the Bank of England of this facility before the British election.
This arrangement with the Bank of England is similar in nature to those which have been made on several occasions among central banks over the last few years in support of various currencies which might at the time have been open to some speculative pressures in the exchange markets. In June 1962, for instance, the Bank of Canada entered into such an arrangement with the federal reserve system and with the Bank of England in support of the Canadian dollar.
The British authorities have not yet announced the amount of the recent new standby arrangements made by the Bank of England or the extent to which the facilities have been used. As I have already said in the house, I do not think there would be any advantage in disclosing here the details of arrangements made on the initiative of another country. The rates of interest applicable under these arrangements have not yet been published by the parties to them, but I am informed they are based on prevailing market rates.

Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet I should like to give an answer to the Leader of the Opposition who, on October 8 and again on October 14 inquired concerning the government's attitude toward deserting seamen. He made specific reference to a number of Greek seamen in Toronto now awaiting hearing of their appeals from convictions handed down by the courts for illegal entry to Canada.
Considerable publicity has been given to the subject of ship deserters, both in the house and in the press, during the past several months, and the problem and difficulties attendant to this question have occupied my department's attention for an even lengthier period. In our review of these problems one point became abundantly clear at the outset; that is that there has been an alarming increase among certain groups of the resort to this particular means of gaining entry to Canada. They are doing so in the hope that even if they are caught they will be able to bring enough public pressure to bear to allow them to remain in this country. These people, the majority of whom are otherwise inadmissible as immigrants, are knowingly and purposely breaking the law, and if this practice were to go unchecked it would only result in utter chaos and a complete disregard for Canadian law.
When discussing the cases referred to by the Leader of the Opposition it must be remembered that there are two separate and distinct issues involved here. In the first instance, because of their actions these persons became the subject of immigration inquiries under the Immigration Act, and were properly ordered deported under section 19 (1) (e) (x) of the act for having remained in Canada without the permission of an immigration officer after the departure of their vessels. In very exceptional cases where the strongest compassionate grounds exist, and where the fullest 

co-operation has been forthcoming, I have directed that the person might be allowed to remain in this country to see how he progresses. I would also like to make it clear, however, that where deportation has taken place this has not ruled out the possibility of the individual being permitted to come forward again at some future date as a legal immigrant in the normal way if he can comply with all other immigration requirements.
As to what may be the outcome of the specific cases referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, it is not possible to say just what action may eventually be taken in their cases. All I can say at the moment is that they will be examined carefully in the light of the policy considerations I have set out above. The specific case of Ilias Vitsas is no different than any of the others, and this man's case will also be carefully reviewed under this policy.
The second issue involved in these cases is that by reason of their method of gaining entry to Canada they have broken the law, and like anyone else who does not adhere to the laws of Canada they become liable for arraignment by the responsible police authorities before the competent courts of the land. It would be inappropriate for me, of course, to offer any comments whatever concerning the action taken or the decisions reached by the courts in these cases.
Regarding the right hon. gentleman's inquiry concerning any direction given to the government's counsel in these cases, I would just like to confirm the position I took earlier in this respect, that no instructions were issued to counsel by either officials of my department or the Department of Justice as to the degree of vigour with which these cases were to be pressed. The role of the prosecuting counsel in these cases was no different than it is in any other court proceeding, and that is to pursue the prosecution only to the point required in the interests of simple justice.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
1. Departmental administration, $6,491,400.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my
intention to make a statement at this time because the estimates of the department have, of course, been thoroughly examined by the standing committee on veterans affairs. I only want to say that I think I should put on the record the fact that I am sure all members of this committee will join with me in expressing our highest commendation for the very efficient and cooperative manner in which the estimates were dealt with in that committee. Perhaps I should also put on the records of the house the resolution moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West in that committee, which is as follows;
I would like to move that this committee express its appreciation of the clear, concise and informative

Supply-Veterans Affairs way in which the deputy minister and other officials have answered questions during this hearing.
I should like to add my commendation to that remark.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to go any further at this moment, because as I said the estimates were thoroughly dealt with in the committee. I will of course answer any questions that are asked during our examination of the estimates this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the fact that the estimates were dealt with quite thoroughly by the committee, but I did anticipate that the minister would make a statement about government policy in respect of veterans affairs at this time. Simply because these estimates were considered thoroughly by a committee does not in itself relieve the minister from his responsibility to indicate on the floor of this chamber, at the beginning of a consideration here of his estimates, what government policy is in respect of veterans affairs. I think the minister should indicate what legislation he has in mind for the veterans of this country. The minister has given us no indication in that regard this afternoon, the first opportunity we have had for a general discussion.
The minister has not satisfied me, nor presumably other members on this side of the house, by simply suggesting that because these estimates were considered thoroughly by a committee it is not necessary for him to make a further statement here. This is the forum in which the government has the opportunity to outline policy in respect of major questions, such as veterans affairs, and the forum in which we have a responsibility to listen and to commend or criticize those policies. I hope that at some later time the minister will consider what I have said in this regard and give us an outline of the government's intentions.
When questions were asked during the committee meetings about legislation or review of legislation in respect of veterans affairs, the minister said he hoped that the government's intentions in respect of this legislation would be introduced in the house by the end of this month or early next month. I am sure the minister must realize, as we do, that the members of this committee are very limited in their approach to this important subject without having in their minds some idea of government policy.
On December 10, 1963, the third report of the standing committee on veterans affairs
[Mr. Teillet.l

was presented to this house. It contained a number of recommendations which called for legislative action. As yet we have not seen evidence of any action of that kind. At this time we can only hope that there will be something done in the way of legislation in respect of veterans affairs. The minister said that there would be some legislation of this kind introduced. I think it would help us in our consideration of these estimates to know what that legislation is.
A period of ten or 11 months has elapsed since that committee report was received by the house. Surely that is sufficient time for the minister to make a review of the veterans legislation and consider the steps which ought to be taken in respect of the recommendations of that committee. Surely the minister has had time to consider the representations that I am sure he has received during that period of time. Obviously there is necessity for a review and revision of veterans legislation. The minister did not enlighten us in this regard by his statement this afternoon. As a result, I think we must consider the recommendations contained in the report of the veterans affairs committee, keeping in mind some of the changes which have occurred since that time. Many of the difficulties which were discussed by the committee have not been sufficiently covered by the minister today.
I should like to refer to two aspects of veterans affairs legislation which were not the subject of recommendations contained in the report to which I have made reference, and I refer to veterans allowances and disability pensions. In view of the substantial increase in the cost of living during the past year, and the various representations which I am sure have been made to the minister and the government-certainly many members of this house have received representations-what consideration is being given to the difficulties being encountered by recipients of war veterans allowances and disability pensions? These recipients are now realizing that their present levels of pensions and allowances are not adequate. We do not know what the government's intention is in this regard. Nothing has appeared on the order paper which would give us an indication. We have been assured that when the legislation does appear on the order paper it will meet all our requirements, but we are not absolutely sure that that is an accurate statement.
In view of the increase in the correspondence received by the members of this

house dealing with this situation, undoubtedly there is a strong realization among the veterans in this country that the present level of pensions and allowances is not sufficient to meet the increased costs they must meet from day to day. Rents have increased as a consequence of increased building costs, about which I think the government has heard a great deal. Food and clothing costs have increased. Because of the fixed level of incomes of veterans, and increasing costs, the veterans are now finding themselves in what our agriculturist friends refer to as a cost-price squeeze. Surely the government has had ample opportunity to do something to alleviate this situation, or at least to give the veterans some assurance that action is contemplated.
I should now like to refer to the recommendations contained in the report of the standing committee on veterans affairs, as presented to the house on December 10, 1963. Recommendation No. 9 in that third report to this house is as follows:
Your committee feels that the time has come when major pieces of pensions legislation should be reviewed and is of the opinion that much of the difficulty can be overcome by reviewing the sections in question so as to clarify the following points:
(a) "Benefit of doubt". At the moment there is some evidence to show that the interpretation now being given by the commissioners is not sufficiently broad to be entirely in keeping with what we believe to be the spirit of the act.
We suggest that the word "doubt" in the phrase "benefit of doubt" be interpreted to mean "a reasonable doubt" as might be expected to arise in the mind of a reasonable man in the street.
As the minister is well aware, this question about the benefit of doubt was raised during the deliberations of the committee. The chairman of the pension commission said that the benefit of doubt in his opinion is adequately exercised in reviewing every case that comes before the commission. We do not doubt the sincerity of the chairman of the pension commission in that regard. We believe that within the general terms of reference to that commission they do exercise the benefit of the doubt. I am sure there is not one member of this house who does not have a thick file of representations from veterans in respect of applications for pension or revisions of pension. As a result I am sure most members have come to the conclusion that the benefit of the doubt clause has not been exercised as generously as has been suggested, or as generously as we in this house think it ought to be. We do not think it is being exercised as
Supply-Veterans Affairs generously as was intended by the parliament of Canada when it enacted the legislation which contains that clause.
I should like to refer to a specific case, and there have been a great many over the last six or seven years. An individual of the Royal Canadian Navy while on board a vessel in the port of New Orleans between 1943 and 1944 underwent an appendix operation. From that time he has had a history of continuous illness, both while in the service and after his discharge, including tuberculosis, which resulted in a period of confinement in a t.b. sanitorium. This was followed by bouts of blindness, deafness and continuous pain. The veteran required drugs over a period of many years, all of which he paid for. No help was provided in this regard through any pension award because no benefit of the doubt was given. Unfortunately the doctors were unable to come to a final diagnosis of the disease and because they could not diagnose the disease they would not give an opinion whether it was as a consequence of war service. But one fact that was known was that the recurring illness was continuous from the time the man had the initial operation while on service until the time he applied to the pension commission. Finally after 18 years the pension commission did grant a pension but made it retroactive for only 12 months.
Where is there adequate application of the benefit of the doubt in such a case? This is what the committee had in mind when it asked the government to consider reviewing the legislation in order to provide a far more generous interpretation of the phrase "benefit of doubt" and far greater attention to the needs of the veterans in order to eliminate cases of the kind I have just cited, where years and years can elapse and the veteran is perhaps finally given pension entitlement only as a consequence of the exercise of the benefit of the doubt. But how many years of suffering, financial uncertainty, job loss and agony of mind must a veteran go through before the benefit of the doubt is applied in the manner in which the parliament and government of Canada meant it should be applied, I believe, when this provision was placed in the legislation?
I go on to the second part of recommendation No. 9 in the committee report where in paragraph (b) they state:
That the burden of proof rests with the commission and not with the veteran applicant.
Then there is a reference to an extract from Lord Denning's report which appears in the
9288	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs evidence during the committee's hearings last year. I believe it is up to the minister to tell us very soon whether these recommendations have been fully considered and whether legislation is going to be presented to us based upon them. He should also tell us why it has been found necessary to bring forward the general discussion of veterans affairs on these estimates before the legislation has been made available to the house for study. Section 10 of the committee's report reads as follows:
Your committee further feels that instead of a "one-shot" appeal which is both final and binding, there should be two appeals as follows:
(a)	a preliminary appeal in which all the evidence is transcribed and then the ruling is given in the form of a written judgment in which all points of evidence both medical and legal on which the ruling is based is set forth in writing and signed.
In the committee we heard officers of the department say that when a final judgment is given by the commission the veteran is acquainted with all of the facts and knows the reasons for the commission's decision. Although I do not deny that this information is available, I am not certain that those who have made applications and receive word of rejection are completely aware of all of the reasons. If they are, if they know the procedures to follow, if it is common knowledge among these people what they must do next, then how is it that so many members of parliament spend so much of their time endeavouring to secure answers for them? There is not one member of the house who does not have case after case in which he finds himself acting as an intermediary between the veteran and the minister and his departmental officials.
If the means by which veterans are informed of their rights and of the reasons for the rejection of pension applications are adequate, surely there should be no necessity for the voluminous quantity of mail in this regard with which members of parliament have to deal. There must be something missing in the procedures. Surely it would be a very simple matter to improve the procedures so that veterans who make application to the commission will have a far better understanding of the precise reasons for rejection, what they have to do next and how to go about entering an appeal. The second part of recommendation No. 10 in last year's report reads as follows:
(b)	a second ruling as at present. Your committee recommends that this procedure would correct the disadvantage the veteran now suffers as


he would know what arguments must be rebutted instead of having to prepare his appeal blindly as at present.
It may be that the committee report goes a little too far. In my experience the chief pensions advocate and the pensions advocates across the country do a remarkable job in helping veterans to present their appeals. Once the pensions advocates become familiar with the case and get in touch with the veteran their work on behalf of the veteran is outstanding. They give very sympathetic attention to these matters and I do not believe they permit veterans to go blindly into appeals.
However, strangely enough, although we are assured that the procedures are well understood by all applicants we find that time and time again members of parliament must intervene in order to bring a veteran who does not seem to know his rights into contact with the officers of the department, including the veterans advocates, who can assist him. Therefore in this instance it is perhaps not so much a failure of administration or policy but a failure of communication. If this is all that is missing, then for goodness sake let us get something done about it because it does not need to wait for legislation. This is an administrative matter that can be taken care of.
Because of the substantial volume of mail that members continually receive, I am afraid it is not going to be enough to suggest to members that the present procedures are adequate. Furthermore, I am sure the minister knows from his own experience, as do his departmental officials, that the mail we receive is not frivolous. It does not involve somebody trying to get something for nothing. The Legion branches and other veterans organizations do very valuable work in this regard, and time and time again when cases are brought to the attention of members of the house or the Legion it turns out that the applicant has not understood his rights and has finally approached a Legion branch or another veterans organization or a member of the house in order to try to get proper attention to his legitimate rights. A failure of understanding has intervened and has been the cause of considerable hardship and suffering for some veterans when in fact procedures exist to relieve such conditions.
The eleventh recommendation of the committee was in these words:
Your committee is of the opinion that the time has come when the excellent prosthetic service developed by the D.V.A. should become a national service available for all Canadians.

It would be interesting to know how far the government has proceeded in looking into that question, and I believe other speakers may be dealing with it in more detail later today. The twelfth recommendation reads as follows:
Your committee is aware that a point has been reached where a decision must be made regarding treatment services in both areas of responsibility and administration. Your committee recommends that fullest consultation be carried out with veterans organizations before any changes are made.
During the past year and a half we have had a good deal of discussion of this question in the house. I believe we can accept the fact that the minister is now consulting in advance with the veterans organizations and he has given the committee the assurance that he will do so in the future, for which we give him full credit. However, as the minister must be aware, if there should be any deviation from this intention there are members of the house who will have something further to say on the question. In view of the testimony given in the committee and what we have heard in answer to questions in the house I believe we can assume that the interests of the veterans are paramount in any change that is contemplated, that their interests will be given first consideration and that the veterans organizations will be consulted prior to any change.
I hope the minister has taken fully into account the recommendation that was made with regard to the payment of increases in veterans pensions and allowances. The recommendation of the committee was to the effect that such changes should be favourably considered whenever similar adjustments are made to the salaries of civil servants and members of the armed services, and consideration should be given to legislation which would bring this about. This would have the result of eliminating increases in pensions and allowances by the sort of hit or miss method that is used at the present time when other considerations than the ones to which I have referred are taken into account. If the government comes to the conclusion that the salaries of civil servants or members of the armed services are not adequate, they act. The procedures in this respect have been greatly altered and a continuous review now takes place. A similar procedure should be adopted with regard to war veterans allowances and pensions. Perhaps the minister has given approval to this idea or something like it, but we do not know. Again, I can only say that it is unfortunate we do not know because
Supply-Veterans Affairs we expected we would know before these estimates came before us.
Finally, there is a very special recommendation in this report upon which I should like to comment. It reads as follows:
In view of the special problems that time and experience have revealed concerning the Hong Kong veterans this committee urges that a special study and survey be made of their problems and particular disabilities.
We understand that such a survey is taking place within the pension commission or within the department. How much longer is it going to take? It has been ten months since this report was made and approximately 20 years since the Hong Kong veterans were brought back to Canada and the Canadian people and the department became aware of the special problems confronting them. During the last year or two, perhaps for a longer period, I do not believe there has been very much new ascertained within the Department of Veterans Affairs about the particular problems of the Hong Kong veterans. The diseases to which they were subjected and the conditions under which they were imprisoned were so severe that a much higher proportion of these prisoners of war have died during the years since the war than in any other particular group of veterans. They are living with continuing afflictions resulting from the diseases and conditions of their environment, their diet, the treatment they received and the things to which they were subjected and from which they have been unable to recover physically, and in many cases mentally as well.
I would expect the minister to be particularly sympathetic because of his own experience. I shared the somewhat similar experience myself in a German camp. I am one of the lucky ones and I expect the minister would consider he is one of the lucky ones, too. The Hong Kong veterans are not lucky. I do not suppose it was ever really lucky to be a prisoner of war, anyway. However, the Hong Kong veterans did encounter particularly difficult circumstances. We know the survey is being made. What are the results? There have been interviews, discussions and questions on this subject in the public forum for years. I feel it is time now we knew what it is the government intends to do. Is this survey going to go the way of so many surveys, and disappear into the limbo of pigeonholes? Let us have some answers. There have been sufficient months now in which to secure and correlate all the information. Give us some indication of the
9290	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs government's intention with regard to the Hong Kong veterans. I am sure there is no member in this house who would not regard sympathetically any action by the government in this regard.
Generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, these are the questions that come to the minds of the members of this committee in dealing with these estimates. Of course it is quite possible that details may be raised on individual items as we go along. One of the things that occurs to us now is that sufficient time has elapsed for us to be made aware of the government's intentions with regard to vetei'ans legislation. We are no longer satisfied to sit here quietly and wait while the government continues to use up further months making up its mind. We want to know now. We want to know precisely what the intentions are and when they are going to be implemented.
So far as the members of the Department of Veterans Affairs are concerned, the senior officers and other officers there, I think it was stated very well in the committee, and it could be repeated here, that every one of us knows the men and women who direct the affairs of the department are dedicated to the interests of the veteran. They have the support of this house in their efforts, regardless of where a member sits. We appreciate what they do, and we will support them in the doing of it. We do want some policy announcement now from the government.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, I was somewhat disappointed that the minister did not take the opportunity in introducing his estimates to inform the house of the government's intentions with regard to amendments to legislation which have been sought by veterans organizations and members of the house for some time. I trust that this brief, shall I say, prologue on his part only indicates we shall hear much more when we come to the epilogue so far as these estimates are concerned. I do want to say this to the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke: I trust he shows the same vigour in protecting the rights of veterans whose property is about to be flooded by the Columbia river development as he has shown this afternoon with regard to these estimates. I can say that in all sincerity because I have had correspondence with many of them. I trust he shows the same sense of urgency in protecting the property and civil rights of 

these veterans against the British Columbia power authority.
Having said that, I want to say that I appreciate the courtesies I have received from the minister. I say quite frankly I have appreciated his personal attention to any questions I have brought before him. I believe that applies as well to inquiries directed to the officials as well. I should like to pay tribute also to the senior officials in Ottawa of all branches of the Department of Veterans Affairs and to the field staff. I support the remarks made by the previous speaker in that respect. There is no question about the services rendered by the officials of this department who, I think it is safe to say, throughout the years have dealt directly with more human beings than any other department of government.
Now, before proceeding, I want to pay tribute to the work of the Royal Canadian Legion, the army and navy veterans association, the Canadian corps, the imperial veterans, the amputation association, the Hong Kong veterans association, and all of those other veteran organizations, who have studied veterans problems so closely. These organizations have made it possible for this department, with the experience of 20 years, to accomplish a great deal for veterans and their dependants. I should like to say that this department is a rather unusual one. ft is the department responsible for providing services to the veterans and their dependants. This has been a great experience so far as Canada is concerned. This department has pioneered legislation that has shown the way for the development of legislation in social welfare, and so on. The department has pioneered certain medical research, as well as the question of manufacturing artificial limbs and that sort of thing, which has been of advantage to Canadians other than veterans. It has pioneered in the treatment service as well. It has pioneered administrative services-administrative procedures and methods. Moreover the Veterans Land Act administration pioneered certain things in connection with farm credit. It is my opinion that the farm credit legislation which was placed on the statute books a few years ago was largely based on the experience of the Veterans Land Act administration.
I have always taken a personal interest in the work of this department and the problems it has to deal with. I am, I believe, well into my twentieth year as a member of the committee on veterans affairs, more recently known as the standing committee on veterans

affairs, and I am sure that when the time comes for me to create a breath of fresh air by disappearing from this chamber I shall be able to say with the poet Moore:
When Time who steals my years away Shall steal my pleasures, too,
Fond memories of these days will stay And half my joys renew.
I wish now to deal briefly with a few of the matters which have been considered by the veterans organizations, by the standing *committee on veterans affairs and by a good many members of this house. Time will not permit me to deal fully with all the questions which concern veterans and veterans organizations. However, I expect colleagues of mine in tnis group to discuss other matters which are of importance. I wish to deal first of all with a resolution which has passed at the last national convention of the Royal [DOT]Canadian Legion. I think this is a matter to which the minister should give some consideration. I will read it:
Whereas Canada achieved nationhood in large measure through the efforts and sacrifice of those who served in the forces in time of war; and
Whereas the Royal Canadian Legion is composed of many ethnic groups which comprise a large portion of Canada's population:
Be it resolved that we urge upon the government that the Royal Canadian Legion be represented on all national committees that may be set up for the purpose of considering Canada's status as a nation.
I support the principle of that motion and 1 support the thought behind it. However, I would suggest it might be advisable to ask all the veterans organizations to get together and nominate persons who could serve on these national committees. I think the veterans of this country should have representation on these important committees which deal with the national questions mentioned and I urge the minister to give this resolution his consideration since I believe it to be very constructive and appropriate.
I wish to turn briefly to the question of pension rates. When the veterans legislation was first under consideration it was established that pensions would be related to the earnings of the ordinary workers of this country. I think this has been the generally accepted principle throughout the years. In recent years there has been an increase in the cost of living across this nation. Salaried people and wage earners have received a measure of compensation by way of increases in salaries and wages. Naturally the veterans organizations have been urging the government to consider granting an increase in disability pension rates. I support such requests
Supply-Veterans Affairs and I support the recommendation of the standing committee on veterans affairs that these rates should be increased to meet the circumstances of the day. We are looking forward with a great deal of anticipation to the introduction of legislation to amend the Pension Act.
There is too this question of the benefit of the doubt, which has been brought before the committee on veterans affairs on a number of occasions. I think this is one of the most contentious and longstanding problems with which the committee has had to deal. We listened last year to the evidence given by the chairman of the Canadian pension commission and we have also listened to the evidence presented by the veterans organizations. The representations of these organizations convinced members of the committee that the benefit of the doubt was not being given in accordance with the expectations of members of parliament when the bill was passed. A recommendation to this effect was included in the committee's last report to the house; I will not deal at great length with this question because one of my hon. friends will be discussing it in greater detail.
Another matter which came before the committee was a request that there should be automatic pension increases for all 50 per cent pensioners on the basis of age. The resolution passed at the convention reads as follows:
Whereas veterans in receipt of 50 per cent pensions for conditions other than gunshot wounds are also experiencing diminished earning capacity:
Therefore be it resolved that all 50 per cent disability pensioners be entitled to the automatic age increase.
I support that resolution, as do other members of our party. I have felt throughout the years that there was a measure of injustice in the working of this section of the Pension Act. I am aware that in the first instance the section was included so as to provide a measure of compensation for those who were wounded in battle. But I think there are many veterans who suffered disabilities in similar circumstances, on the field of battle or otherwise, and I would therefore urge that consideration be given to this proposal also.
An hon. member who spoke earlier mentioned the survey now being undertaken by the department in connection with the needs and circumstances of the Hong Kong veterans. I join with all others in expressing the hope that this survey will soon be complete and that there will be a report followed by some action on the part of the government to meet the needs of these men. In this connection let me say again that one of my hon. friends will

Supply-Veterans Affairs be dealing with the question of these veterans at great length later on.
Another matter in which I am particularly interested is the resolution passed at the last dominion convention of the Royal Canadian Legion to the following effect:
Whereas it appears that the Canadian pension commission from time to time adopts matters of policy in deciding pension cases which are not anywhere stated in law or by regulation:
Therefore be it resolved that whenever any new policy is decided by the commission in dealing with any case, the same shall be made available to the Royal Canadian Legion.
And that all present existing policy which is not stated by regulation or law also be made similarly available.
I strongly support this resolution and I believe this information should be made available to veterans organizations. I recall some years ago requests being made year after year on behalf of veterans organizations that the table of disabilities be made public. This was denied by successive governments. Finally-and I consider this one of my major achievements since I have been a member of this house-I moved a motion for the production of papers asking that this table of disabilities be produced. There was a certain timidity and hesitation on the part of the government of the day, but finally the minister took the bull by the horns and said he was agreeable to the production of the table. It was produced, and it is available now to the veterans organizations of this country. It has been a most valuable document to them. Though there was a certain reluctance about producing it, it is admitted now-I think the minister and his officials will admit it-that it has been a useful document for veterans organizations and their advocates to have in presenting the claims of veterans before the pension commission. I suggest that this further recommendation is very worth while and its implementation would be a positive contribution toward the co-operation that has existed throughout the years between the department and the veterans organizations in Canada in the administration of veterans legislation.
I now come to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I want to make a plea for the consideration of an increase in the war veterans allowance, on the same grounds upon which an increase in disability pensions is being sought. It is obvious from the interest taken in this question by veterans organizations at national, provincial and branch levels that this is a matter of serious concern to the many veterans and their dependants

who do require a substantial increase in the war veterans allowance. I know from personal experience in meeting a good many veterans throughout the constituency that there is a definite need for such an increase. I have discussed with the veterans their difficulties; I know their problems and the domestic circumstances of a good many of the veterans I have the honour to represent, and I have no hesitation in saying, in association with other members in this house, that those veterans on war veterans allowance urgently need an increase in the allowance.
I suggest that at the same time there should be an increase in the permissive income. I think the minister indicated to the committee that this question is receiving some consideration. I am of the opinion that there should be the abolition of the means test in respect of those veterans over age 65. We have never been able to secure general approval for this proposal, but I believe that for those over 65 years of age there should be the abolition of the means test in connection with war veterans allowance.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I come to the question of veterans hospitals. The policy announced by the minister has caused some concern in veterans organizations across this country. First of all I want to congratulate the minister on the way he presented his case before the dominion convention of the Royal Canadian Legion. I fully expected to see a bit of fireworks there. I sat in the audience and listened to him, and I thought he presented his case in such a way that it indicated he knew the spirit and temper of veterans. I heard a good many delegates to that convention, while not agreeing with all the minister said, speak in quite complimentary tones of his very tactful and, shall I say, gracious approach to a prickly problem.
Don't embarrass him.

After the minister had
spoken, that convention passed the following resolution:
Whereas many veterans with chronic disabilities must have domiciliary care and frequently must have expert medical advice as is evidenced from a further statement made by the director-general of treatment services that "they all have some degree of medical reason for being in the hospital and many of them have a very great degree of medical reason":
Therefore be it resolved that no transfer of any D.V.A. hospital to civilian administration be made by D.V.A. at the present time without full consultation at the outset of negotiations and mutual agreement with both dominion and provincial commands of the Royal Canadian Legion; and

Be it further resolved that no such operational transfer be effected until adequate domiciliary care, with the necessary medical services actually in being; and that if and when any active treatment hospital facilities are shared with civilian authorities, D.V.A. must control the admission, the care and the discharge of all veterans, and provision must be made for their admittance, regardless of the pressure of civilian demands.
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I think all reasonable people recognize that there are changing circumstances with respect to admissions to veterans hospitals across this country. I hope and trust that the minister will, in dealing with this problem, recognize the spirit and purpose of the resolution passed by the Royal Canadian Legion. Personally I am quite optimistic in that respect.
Now I come to the Veterans Land Act. A resolution was passed by the Royal Canadian Legion in this connection. I am just picking a few resolutions out of the many that were passed, because they are of particular interest. There was one with respect to the removal of the time limit for serving personnel, which reads as follows:
Whereas it has been determined that many veterans with wartime service now in the Canadian forces are eligible for benefits under the Veterans Land Act:
Therefore be it resolved that the Veterans Land Act be amended to ensure that benefits may be available to veterans now in service upon discharge, regardless of that date.
I think that is a very reasonable request on the part of the Royal Canadian Legion, and the members of this group support it. We look forward to an amendment to the Veterans Land Act to meet the situation that is covered by this resolution. I could go on at greater length to some other minor amendments with respect to the Veterans Land Act, Mr. Chairman, but I will leave those to a later date.
I now come to a question that has been concerning veterans organizations and a good many veterans generally across Canada. This is the question of the maintenance of the veterans preference in the civil service. We will soon be 20 years away from the last world war, veterans are aging, and there is a tendency on the part of some people to feel that the veterans preference should no longer apply, and so on. But, Mr. Chairman, we strongly support the maintenance of the veterans preference in the civil service. The resolution passed by the Royal Canadian Legion dealing with this matter says:
Therefore be it resolved that the existing statutory preferences for war veterans as set out in the Civil Service Act be maintained.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
They were very concerned about the Heeney report of December, 1958, and the Glassco report of July, 1962, which recommended the substitution of a less embracing form of veterans preference for the existing absolute preference. The Royal Canadian Legion also recommended that additional preference be established for world war II veterans. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas these veterans do not qualify for veterans preference over a non-veteran for employment in the federal civil service:
Therefore be it resolved that section 40 of the Civil Service Act be amended to provide an additional veterans preference after the overseas preference to the active veterans of world war II, regardless of where the veteran served.
I trust the minister will give consideration to that recommendation. Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on behalf of the corps of commissionaires. A resolution was passed at the Royal Canadian Legion convention in this regard. I discussed this matter with a number of the delegates present at the convention who are concerned with the growing practice of government departments and private employers in employing private detective agencies. As a matter of fact I was rather shocked when I visited the national art gallery recently and noticed that the building is policed by a private detective agency; I think it is called the national security service, or something of that sort. This has caused veterans some concern, because it reduces the opportunities for veterans who are getting on in years to undertake useful employment and provide a useful service that is not beyond their physical capacity.
In this connection the Legion passed a resolution which is critical of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation because it replaced the corps of commissionaires in certain areas. It says amongst other things:
Whereas a great many veterans who were employed with the corps of commissionaires carrying out these duties have consequently lost their employment; and
Whereas the Legion is becoming increasingly concerned over the failure of governments at all levels to maintain the provisions of the veterans' preference and to promote the employment of ex-servicemen in government positions:
Therefore be it resolved that the government be requested to immediately halt any further replacement of corps of commissionaires personnel by private security agencies and urge other levels of government to follow suit.
I am sure all members of our standing committee on veterans affairs will support that recommendation by the Legion and I urge the minister to look into the question to see

Supply-Veterans Affairs what is happening at the present time. Because this practice of employing private detective agencies is growing.
I know my time is fairly short but I want to make reference now to a matter which concerns veterans in my own constituency. I have raised the matter in the standing committee on veterans affairs. I am referring to those veterans who will be affected by the building of dams under Columbia river treaty projects. There are two classes of veterans: There are those who are purchasing property, but have not completed their purchase from the Veterans Land Act administration, and those who have purchased it in other ways. I think this provides an opportunity for the department to set a pattern which will be of value to the other property owners who will be affected.
At this time I want to thank the minister for his prompt attention to a matter which 1 brought up by way of a question asked in the house. I am informed that the B.C. power and hydro authority soon got wind of the question and answer and immediately sent their men in to meet this veteran in question, to settle the matters of which he complained. These were not matters of price but matters of inconvenience and that sort of thing which I thought were thoroughly unnecessary. Anyway the matters were settled and I thank the minister for his prompt attention and the complete reply I received from him in this respect.
I think the department can perform a service to the veterans who come under its jurisdiction, namely those who still owe money on their properties under the Veterans Land Act administration, and also other veterans and property holders who are affected. I know that a good many of my colleagues in the house think I get a little too disturbed about this question, but I am representing people some of whom I have known for 50 years and the majority of whom I have known for many years. I urge the minister to make certain that everything is done to protect the rights of these veterans under the V.L.A. because, as we were informed in the committee by the director, who I am sure is most sympathetic, the Veterans Land Act administration could not agree to the sale of the property unless the veteran concerned gave his permission. If he failed to give permission, then as a last resort the administration had to get an order in council. I hope that the Department of Veterans Affairs stands right up squarely for the veterans who are depending on them.	-	:; n .

In this connection I want to read a letter written by a veteran who lives in the riding of Okanagan-Revelstoke. This letter was published in the Revelstoke Review on Thursday, October 15 last, and I have received numerous letters in similar vein to this from people living up and down the shores of the Columbia river and along the Arrow lakes, both veterans and other property owners. I mention this letter because this indicates the spirit of the B.C. power and hydro authority. The letter says:
Editor, Review:
Farmers in Sidmouth are now facing the darkest time in their lives. Soon we will be forced to leave our farms and homes at hydro's price.
There is no bargaining on their part; B.C. hydro sets the price and people have to take it or leave it. There is no negotiation. The letter continues:
We have nothing to say even if we have lived here 50 to 60 years, worked hard and made a place for ourselves where we could make a living as long as we live.
If that is just around the corner for us, 42,000 Canadians who died for freedom must be turning in their graves at this display of freedom and civil rights.
That figure is wrong; it should be 60,000 odd.
We might as well join the 42,000, as there is little to live for now.
We know we are living in an awful troubled world, but the Bible tells us that the time will soon be here when the lion will eat with the lamb- instead of now-when the lion eats the lamb.
That is the B.C. power and hydro authority to which he is referring.
