I appreciate the courtesy of hon. members. This letter concludes:
The present situation in our valley shows that water is getting more and more expensive and our farms less and less valuable.
I mention that because it is typical of the letters I have received from veterans; and I received another the other day from a veteran near Castlegar. It is obvious that people would not write in this vein unless they thought they were being treated unfairly and

unjustly and I urge the department to do what they can to help these veterans.
There is one more matter before I conclude. There is a veterans cemetery in the area, with individual veterans graves. I trust that the department will do all it can to see that the rights and wishes of relatives are respected. I hope they will make an investigation to see what cemeteries will be affected and what individual graves in other cemeteries will be affected; and I hope the department will do all it can to ease the difficulties of the veterans who are affected by this development.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I want to say we appreciate the fact that the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs were referred to the committee for detailed study and analysis. I believe this gives an opportunity for a more thorough examination of the details of the estimates which are contained in the blue book. I was rather surprised at one or two references today to the absence of any extended remarks by the minister. It was my understanding that reference of estimates to a committee was not only to help expedite a thorough study of the estimates but also somehow to reduce the necessity of extended debate when they came back to the house; but perhaps my understanding is not quite true to the fact in this connection. However, I do not intend to prolong the debate on the estimates at this time, although I do want to make several brief references to a number of items of special concern which have been referred to me by constituents and others from time to time.
In the course of the committee hearings the Minister of Veterans Affairs indicated that amendments would be introduced to a variety of acts concerning veterans, and perhaps I was rather naive but I expected him to come through with them in due course. However, this afternoon it was pointed out that we have not anything at all in this regard except the minister's says so. We have nothing definite or positive, so therefore we are somewhat held in suspense. As I pointed out on another occasion, I think we have to take the minister's words at face value, and we expect in the very near future to have him bring before this house the amendments he has predicted and promised concerning various acts having to do with veterans affairs.
Mr. Chairman, reference has been made this afternoon to the possibility and desirability of an increase in war veterans allow-
Supply-Veterans Affairs ances, and I should like to give my full support to this request. It is not necessary to enlarge upon it or state once again the reasons for this request, but perhaps I should clarify the situation. There are two factors which ought to be taken into consideration. One is the constantly increasing cost of living, and the second is the upward revision of pensions that are being paid to Canadian citizens through other types of legislation. These two reasons alone would be sufficient to support an upward revision of war veterans allowances. Therefore when the minister does introduce amendments I trust one will deal with this matter.
Another matter in this same connection which has been brought to my attention on a number of occasions by veterans is the necessity for amendment relating to the service-related disability pensions. There is a strong feeling that these have been somewhat bypassed, and a number of veterans feel they had been completely left out in the cold. On their behalf I recommend that consideration be given to veterans who fall within this specific category.
Another request was made for an increase in the ceiling on permissive income. The hon. member for Kootenay West made reference to this particular matter. I do not think there can be any argument as far as this request is concerned, because we are all aware of the increased cost of living, and that with an increase in that cost there is a decrease in the purchasing value of our dollar. That is one of the reasons we have been advocating that, as far as personal income taxes are concerned, there should be an increase in the basic exemption. I believe that is absolutely necessary, and suggest the same principle applies to veterans. Veterans require more in order to maintain the standard of living which they have been used to. I was going to say the standard of living which they have enjoyed in the past, but perhaps I should not go that far. In drafting his legislation I would ask the minister to remember these veterans and bring in some definite recommendation or proposal in respect of an increase in the ceiling on permissive income of veterans.
There is just one other matter I should like to bring to the attention of this committee, although I was not very successful when I broached this subject during a meeting of the veterans affairs committee. I have reference to the quite general dissatisfaction in regard to decisions handed down by the pension commission. I was given to understand most of the personnel on the pension

Supply-Veterans Affairs commission are veterans and are bending over backwards to accommodate veterans, to the extent of bending the regulations almost to the breaking point. There is considerable room for improvement in this particular respect.
Reference was made to the benefit of doubt clause, and perhaps that is one of the most important issues to be considered, because like many other members of parliament 1 have received communications and briefs outlining the positions in which many veterans find themselves. In view of the method by which appeals from decisions of this commission are considered one could hardly expect the decisions to be altered. Looking at these decisions from the point of view expressed in the many representations we have received we can only feel that in many cases far better treatment could have been accorded to those individuals who have applied for pension or who have asked for revisions of their pension benefits. In this connection I suggest the minister should give close and diligent attention to this aspect of veterans problems. As was pointed out during the meetings of the veterans affairs committee, the greatest number of complaints and gripes lodged by veterans relates to this aspect of their problems. That being the case, it would seem to me that there must be some justification for this attitude of dissatisfaction toward decisions rendered by the pension commission.
As I pointed out earlier, Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to prolong the debate on these estimates, but I did feel that I should bring these points to which I have referred to the attention of the minister, and to give my support to the various suggestions which have been raised and which will no doubt be raised by hon. members during the course of this debate.

At this stage in the study of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs, I would like to make a short remark concerning the difference which exists between the veterans, or the active army, and the servicemen who serve in this country in peacetime.
I must point out that the minister and the government pay special attention to veterans, and I realize that this is necessary. In my opinion, there is surely room for improvements, and I realize that the minister, with his understanding and good will, is giving consideration to those future improvements.


But if some of our men who were on active service, whether on the battlefield or not, have recognized rights, we should also think about those who serve in this country in peacetime.
When a soldier serves overseas for a period of one, two or five years, or even only one year or six months, he has some rights. One realizes that those who serve in peacetime for periods of five, eight and even 11 years, do not get the same attention.
I therefore ask the minister to give more attention to our soldiers serving in Canada in peacetime, so that when for some reason or other they leave the army, they will not suffer hardships and have to rely on social welfare to provide for their needs. This is the recommendation I wished to make to the minister at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to congratulate the minister upon his courtesy in always giving immediate attention to questions directed to him. I do not intend to prolong this debate for any length of time, but I do feel that I should express my hope that there will be no further encroachments on veterans hospitals across Canada. This is a day and age when we need more research centres. By and large, the veterans hospitals have proven to be great reservoirs for research.
It is almost 20 years now since the end of the last war, and it is obvious that most of the veterans of that war are over 40 years of age, although of course, there are some younger veterans of the Korean war. The illnesses and injuries these veterans suffered during combat, and for which they now require treatment, are becoming chronic and more disabling. It follows that the majority of cases will fall under the following headings: cardiovascular renal disease, chest cases, cancer, prosthetic cases or the effects of wounds and contusions suffered in battle.
Hospitals are established by the Department of Veterans Affairs for research purposes, the training of interns and as teaching centres in postgraduate work. All of the active treatment hospitals with which I am familiar are approved by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada and this puts the stamp on them to indicate that they are number one, so far as the training of personnel is concerned. In that regard I am not only referring to doctors. We are going to be very short of doctors quite soon. In fact, doctors are in short supply right now but the

need is going to increase over and over again. The same thing applies to personnel such as laboratory technicians, radiology technicians and so forth right down the line.
It is interesting to note that there are 270 doctors taking training in veterans hospitals across Canada and that there are over 157 interns in occupational therapy, physiotherapy, psychology and laboratory work. Another interesting fact is that there are some 90 research projects under way. If we are going to set up more medical schools across Canada, surely one of the things we must have is more trained personnel. We have to have more people who have done research work and have become professors because we are short now of such personnel.
A great many of the projects appeal to all of us because they are in the field of geriatrics, and there is not one of us in this house who is not getting older. In this field of course investigation is concerned with arteriosclerosis and why people develop it. This is in the news today because all one has to do is to visit the old people's homes and chronic invalid hospitals across Canada and he will see people being cared for there day after day at great expense to the taxpayers. I am trying to focus attention on the fact that if through research we can prevent the development of this disease we will have done a lot to relieve the burden that the taxpayer has to bear today, to say nothing of the suffering of the people involved, which is of course the greatest of all considerations.
Geriatrics also is concerned with the field of coronary disease and strokes. I am sure that all of us have friends or even members of our own families who have had a coronary attack or a small stroke. We see the mental ability of people who suffer strokes one after the other slipping away, unless something is done to keep the condition under control.
As I have said, our chronic hospitals are loaded with victims of these diseases. Surely the veterans hospitals are doing a worthwhile work from a dollars and cents point of view. This point is not emphasized enough. If the work they do can prevent a person suffering from a chronic disease having to be placed in an old persons home or chronic hospital where somebody has to look after him and where he becomes a complete and total liability, then they are certainly doing a great job in reducing the cost, to say nothing about restoring the happiness of the individual.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
In cutting down the number of veterans hospitals are we leaving out of consideration the rights of the veterans, the promises made to them and our debt to them? After all, there would not be a Canada today if they had not gone overseas and fought for this country. I am going to be brief but I want to draw the attention of the minister to the question of the application of the benefit of the doubt provision. I recall the case of a man who was receiving $8 a month in war veterans allowance. He had been ill for years and was unable to work. His wife went out and worked and maintained the home. She had to have a car to operate her business and she brought somebody into the house to look after her husband when he needed care.
If my memory serves me correctly, this man was awarded a war veterans allowance of approximately $8 a month. In addition, his hospitalization was paid for as well as his doctor bills and his drugs. This man has been in and out of hospital four or five times over the years to my own knowledge. When he was well enough that he could go home he was sent home for his wife to look after him and she did so and got help when she needed it. She did a very good job. When he became acutely ill again from his cardiovascular renal disease he had to go back into the hospital and be given oxygen treatment. He was treated many times in this way but after four weeks or so in an acute illness hospital the hospital wanted to get rid of him, so he was sent home again. Not once was he put into an institution or home. His wife looked after him.
After this man had received the allowance of $8 a month for two or three years an investigator called and looked into their bank book and a lot of other things. I understand that the wife had not earned over $3,600 in any one year. However, the investigator went to the bank and looked into the matter. The last I heard about the case was that the lady was supposed to pay all the money back. This man is 70 years of age. Where in the name of common sense is there any milk of human kindness or decency in such an action? I bring this case to the attention of the committee as one with which I am familiar and about which I feel very sad, because what has been done is not right. This man is a veteran of the first world war and is now 70 years of age. Those are the facts as I understand them.
I recall the case of another man who is a veteran of the second great war. He was in

Supply-Veterans Affairs the tank corps and was blown up a few times. He was an A-one risk and was in the army for five years. I knew his doctor very well and I asked him about this fellow. His doctor said he was a real hardy buck, just like the whole family. After spending five years overseas this man returned and tried several things but was a failure. Finally he became a patient of a certain doctor. Under any stress or strain this man breaks down. In other words, he was psychologically damaged.
This case was brought before the pension commission. The doctors gave their evidence and said that the man was pensionable. But what pension did they give him? Twenty per cent. With the great upsurge in education today, how in the name of conscience do they expect veterans who fought in the last great war to compete in a world where more and more education is needed and where it is harder and harder to get a job and keep it? This man is unemployable but he was only awarded a 20 per cent pension. This is not right, Mr. Chairman. I appeal to the minister to look into these cases and see to it that a little more of the milk of human kindness is shown. I know there are regulations, but for heaven's sake do not have the regulations completely loaded in favour of one side.
Then, I wanted to dwell for a moment on the problems facing the sons of deceased veterans. I understand they receive $500 per year if they are going to university. If they are going into medicine, which is a six year course, they receive this allowance for only four years. I should like to know if such a student could apply for a student loan under the new legislation and thus secure the extra $500 or $1,000 which may be needed.
In conclusion, I should like to say that I know the minister must be sympathetic to the veterans problems because he has been through the mill himself. Do not let us sit down and make a soldier who went over and fought for us subject to the balancing of a group of statistics, weighing this on one hand and that on the other. Do not let us treat him in that way. We know that the cost of living has gone up. The last time there was an increase in the pension was in 1961 under the previous government. Surely to goodness, when everyone else gets a salary increase or a pension increase, the veteran is entitled to one too. The members of this house have had their salaries increased. Why do we have to leave the veterans to the last? Probably the minister has been thinking about the things along this line that he should 

do, and for heaven's sake let us do them. Let us put the veteran back where he should be. We always seem to be late in looking after the fellow who went over to fight for us.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments to say something about the transfer of military hospitals to civilian authority. I support the previous speaker and say, with great respect, that I feel the minister should look very carefully into the question of the transfer of hospitals. The first question is, what is civilian authority? There is a presumption that there is some overriding authority in every city which controls the administration of hospitals. We know that in Toronto this is not so. Each hospital has its own administrative body. It is a well known fact that a doctor on the staff of one hospital cannot practise in another hospital. It is well known that some hospitals do not release patients on Saturday or Sunday. It is suspected also that some doctors keep their patients in hospital a little longer than necessary because of the system of allocating beds. In fact, the question comes up, how are beds allocated in hospitals? Is it on the basis of seniority in practice or seniority on the staff? Everyone knows that there has been trouble in the larger centres in connection with hospital beds and the shortage of beds. For that reason I feel this department should look into the matter carefully before transferring any veterans hospitals to these-civilian authorities. The administrative control of hospitals should remain with the department.
Then you will also have to face the question of the doctors in the department being paid a salary. If you are going to have another group of doctors who are in business for themselves in these hospitals, you are going to have a conflict of interest. Who is going to be in control? The department should remain in control until there is some satisfactory conclusion of the problem of the shortage of hospital beds. We have discussed these questions in the committee and it is clear that the patients are becoming more and more of one type, either rheumatic or aged. This does not give enough challenge to the doctors. We agree with this. We agree with a lot of the problems that Dr. Crawford has put before us. We agree with him when he says he wants to maintain the highest standards in his treatment centres across Canada.
There is another avenue that perhaps the minister has not explored, and that is to allow veterans hospitals to be used by veterans

and their families. Then the administration of these hospitals could still be maintained by the department. You could have all types of cases in these hospitals and it would also relieve the shortage of beds in other hospitals. Another advantage would be that mentioned by the previous speaker, the opportunity for research and for the development of new ideas in hospitalization. No one in Canada as yet has investigated the concept of hospitals that is quite common now in Switzerland, where they were faced with a shortage of nursing staff, too. With a slightly larger capital outlay, they have constructed duplicate rooms so that the relatives of some patients can live in and do a lot of the nursing chores, thus leaving the nurses free to perform medical chores. This practice has resulted in many people being drawn to the nursing profession. After all, we all admit that a lot of the chores nurses must do are not really medical chores. This is something which I believe the department could investigate in connection with veterans hospitals.
I should like to add this one word of caution to the minister: Do not transfer administrative control of veterans hospitals to the civilian authority, as you call it, until you are absolutely sure that the veterans will get first class treatment, without knowing a doctor or having had a doctor for a certain length of time, without qualification as to the size of his purse or any of these things. A veteran must have the best of treatment immediately. With that note of caution, I just want to say that I have received the greatest co-operation from this department and the minister. He should be proud. There has never been a question left unanswered or a problem left unattended to by this department.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to repeat many of the things that have been said here this afternoon, other than to endorse the idea that it is about time some attention was given to the pensions of veterans, and in particular the recipients of war veterans allowance. As has been said, people who are on a fixed income such as this are completely dependant on this government and this House of Commons to look after their present and future welfare. Certainly the time is long overdue, in the face of the rising cost of living and other circumstances, when some attention should be given to this matter.
I should like also to compliment the minister on the manner in which he deals with
Supply-Veterans Affairs problems. Even when he says no, as he unfortunately has to do on different occasions, he does it in a very nice way. My purpose today is not to criticize this legislation in general but to draw attention to some of its inadequacies. I believe this legislation was passed by people of good will who believed at the time it would be adequate to look after the needs of our veterans. But as time went on we found that loopholes and inadequacies existed, and it is to these that I wish now to draw attention in the hope that action will be taken to correct the situation.
One of the matters which has come to my attention, and I am sure it has come to the attention of other members of this house, is the predicament in which veterans of the first world war who are now in their sixties find themselves. Maybe they have found gainful employment over the years and belonged to various medical plans, either those they have joined in the course of their employment or others which exist across the country. These men are now in their late sixties. When they give up whatever jobs they are engaged in they may lose their medical coverage and find it extremely difficult to get coverage under private plans. This is a situation which calls for attention, and I think the Department of Veterans Affairs should consider whether it would not be possible to make medical and hospital coverage available to these people through a scheme which would cover all veterans reaching an age at which they are denied coverage by the various private plans which exist in this country.
There Is another matter which is of considerable concern to me because I believe that in addition to its unfairness to those involved it is a contradiction of common sense. Consider a recipient of war veterans allowance who does have medical and hospital coverage himself. If he is a married veteran and if he wishes to get coverage for his spouse he finds that in order to do so he has to insure himself as well as his spouse. I feel this is unfair because the Department of Veterans Affairs is already providing medical coverage for the veteran himself. Yet he has to pay a premium for double coverage despite the fact that he, like many other veterans, may be in straitened financial circumstances. I do not think this makes sense. I think it is a situation which should be straightened out. I believe that having regard to the small extra cost which would be involved, coverage should be
9300	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs provided for the spouses of all recipients of war veterans allowance.
This leads me to another problem and it is a much more complicated one. It has to do with recipients of war veterans allowance who still have dependant children. I fully realize that this allowance was originally intended for elderly veterans. But as I have mentioned we find these loopholes occurring from time to time. In recent years we have found that younger veterans, some of them considerably below the age of 60, may through some chain of circumstances, illness or accident, become completely unable to provide for their own living, and the existing legislation has been stretched so as to include these cases under the war veterans allowance provisions. However, no provision can be made for their children and their dependants. I believe something should be done in this connection.
I should like to illustrate this contention by drawing attention to one case which really highlights the loophole which exists in the legislation. I believe the minister is familiar with this case; part of these 61 letters which have accumulated in this file over the last 15 months are letters to his department. I should like to show the committee just what can happen to a veteran and his family under the present legislation. This has to do with a veteran who is only 42 years of age. This man is completely crippled, unable even to walk around, let alone provide any sort of living for himself and his family. As a result of various representations we have been able to establish a partial war veterans allowance which now amounts to $99 a month. In addition I was able to establish through the Ontario department of welfare a partial dependant fathers allowance. But I should like to draw attention to the ordeal through which this particular family has gone in the last 15 months. Aside from the war veterans allowance which has, thank goodness, been stable throughout these months, this is exactly what the family has received; I have the correspondence here to show the amounts to which the provincial department ruled these people were eligible. In September, 1963, they were entitled to $145.20; in October, $145.45; in November, $96.70; in December $45.95; in January $47.20; in February, March and April, $30.25; in May, $9.25; in June, $39.05; in July and August, $54.70, and now, $78.70. It is a miracle to me not only how this family can keep body and soul together but how they can keep their sanity.
Just to make sure I have this straight-the hon. member is not now speaking of the war veterans allowance?
That is correct.
The variations in these amounts are not variations in W.V.A.?

No, the minister is correct. I mentioned earlier that the war veterans allowance of $99 a month has remained stable throughout this period. But I am illustrating the ordeal which veterans and their families are going through under the existing legislation as it applies across the country in cases where they have to turn to two or three different sources in order to try to eke out a minimum standard of living. This is an actual case.
Moreover, some time last June I was able to get the department to reassess this case and the department came to the conclusion that there was a back payment due of $124.20, which they said would be forwarded to the family by the end of June. Well, that cheque arrived less than two weeks ago. In other words, this family was kept dangling on the end of a string for five months waiting for a cheque to come. How can these people budget, how can they have any peace of mind in circumstances such as this? This is why I say that while the veterans legislation in the main is good there are a number of loopholes in the various acts, and these loopholes must be plugged up.
There is one other point I should like to raise in the course of my brief remarks today. It has to do with veterans-possibly only a small number of them-who during their service, particularly overseas, came in contact with certain contagious diseases. I think the contraction of these diseases should be regarded rather as an accident; the attitude taken now is to regard them almost in the same way as a self-inflicted wound. I think that especially where families are involved, where children and dependants are involved -certainly no blame can be laid on a spouse or on the children-something should be done, and the department should take a new look at the way in which these particular problems are handled.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, my criticism is not of the legislation in general but rather of the particular things that crop up from time to time. I am sure every other hon. member is familiar with them, because I do not think the mail on these problems is confined to my office.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up much of the time of the committee because I realize these estimates have been carefully examined by the standing committee on veterans affairs. However,
I would like to make one plea to the minister, and I do not want him or anyone else to get the impression that if I limit my remarks to this one topic I do not agree with some of the views that have been expressed by other members of the committee with regard to the need for reviewing and increasing the scales of pensions and war veterans allowance.
I would like to make a special plea with regard to a special, small group of veterans.
I refer to the survivors of the expedition to Hong Kong in 1941. I think everyone would agree that these men are in a special category. After all, they spent almost four years in prisoner of war camp, where they suffered from malnutrition, and so on. The minister is familiar with the excellent submission of the Hong Kong veterans association made to the veterans affairs committee and I would commend that strongly to him for a further review.
I am aware of the fact that the pension commission is engaged in a survey to determine exactly what the data is with regard to the health, life expectancy, and so on, of this special group of veterans. However, Mr. Chairman, this is a fairly long process and I would urge the minister to give immediate consideration to means of doing something for these veterans to recompense them in some degree for the special suffering they endured. They were in a special category, and still are I believe, because during their time in prisoner of war camp they suffered from malnutrition to an extent not experienced by other veterans. As a result of this, and for other reasons, they contracted diseases which are not even well known in this part of the world, in addition to a great many diseases like beriberi and pellagra, which stem directly from malnutrition. They were undernourished, badly housed, and constantly ill. Nevertheless, during their imprisonment they worked most of the time at hard types of labour such as in the coal mines, shipyards, and so on. In my judgment, Mr. Chairman, this has inevitably left not only physical damage with these veterans, but perhaps more importantly, physchological damage.
I would recommend to the minister that in the case of Hong Kong veterans he should
Supply-Veterans Affairs consider giving them entitlement to free treatment for any illness for the rest of their lives. In many cases these men have an anxiety neurosis, if I use the correct technical term; they are worried about their life expectancy, their constant illness, and so on, which makes it difficult for them to retain a job or leaves them with a fear that they will not succeed in staying in their job for a reasonable period of time.
I believe consideration should also be given to the possibility, in the case of Hong Kong veterans who are receiving veterans disability pension, of providing that their entitlement to pension should not be less than 50 per cent. This would compensate for the general deterioration in their health and I believe it would have a tremendously useful psychological effect, because they would then know their widows would not be left without recourse to assistance if they died prematurely. I commend these matters to the minister's attention.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to say a word or two of appreciation for the devoted and dedicated men throughout the department who have served the veterans between the wars and since. I do not think any government department is to be so highly commended for the way they have looked after the returned soldiers generally. However, times change, and those things that were done for the soldiers 20 years ago are now out of date. I want to touch on just two things. One is the need for a complete review of the situation with regard to veterans pensions. In my opinion section 70 of the act, which in general is a very generous act as we all know, has not been taken by the pension boards in the spirit in which it was passed by this parliament. I might remind the committee that section 70 provides that the benefit of doubt should be given to the veteran in all cases.
I know, from having sat on the committee myself and from having received complaints from veterans generally, that this is their main objection; the veteran feels that before he can make a case for his pension he is obliged to prove, usually with documents, that he did in fact suffer such and such harm to his health, which is attributable to war service. Of course, Mr. Chairman, in a great many cases it is impossible to prove this. Although records were kept while we were in Canada and in England, and often on the battlefield, in a great many cases the records are far from complete, and in some cases the

Supply-Veterans Affairs most deserving veterans are left without any documents whatsoever with which to prove their case. Then they are obliged, generally, to go through a series of long correspondence with their old pals in order to find out who was their doctor, their old buddies in the line, and so on, and by verbal evidence of one form and another establish a case. Even then I am afraid that in some cases they are not given the benefit of the doubt. This is a difficult problem, but I am sure that we as legislators intended that when the veteran has a case which can be believed one way or the other, in simple terms he is to be given the benefit of the doubt. Efforts were made to put through a private bill, Bill No. C-7, but it has not been put through. It purported anyway, to remove the onus from the veteran, and to put into the statute books a clear ruling so the veteran would in all cases be given the benefit of the doubt.
The general cost of living is constantly going up-I know I am being repetitive, but I do not think it can be repeated too often until definite action is taken in this regard-and the circumstances in which we all earn our living in this modern age have changed. At one time, I suppose, say 30 years ago, if a man had today's veterans pension he would have been well off. However, today he is expected to live on it, pay the average rent paid in Canada and support himself alone; and we must all admit that the average pension does not do that in any style at all. Add to that the fact that, although we do not always like to admit it in our affluent society, a large percentage of our women are working, and if a veteran is completely disabled it means that his wife would have to stay at home. Therefore she is cut off from supplementary earnings to assist the modern family. Let us be realistic and realize that a single pension today, or even a married pension, is not adequate to support a home in the way intended.
The next point I want to make concerns the Hong Kong veterans. It is argued that the Hong Kong veterans should be treated exactly the same as anybody else. That is what people have said; but I personally have known some of these veterans over the past 20 years, and although I am not a doctor I would say without hesitation that the greater percentage of these boys have had their physical ability-and I stress physical ability because it is that on which all pensions are based -to earn their living in a pioneer country like Canada in most cases, I would say, reduced by at least 50 per cent. If there is nothing specifically wrong with them, such

as having had a broken arm or having lost their eyesight, something which can be definitely assessed, it is very difficult to say how much pension they should get. This group have asked in their brief for a 50 per cent pension for every veteran taken prisoner in Hong Kong. I would not go so far as to say that every man who served in Hong Kong has had his physical capacity to earn his living reduced, but this is certainly one case where section 70 should be applied.
Let us say a Hong Kong veteran complains of continuous fatigue. In this case his employer could be interviewed and if his employer said that he was one of the most willing men on the staff, but that he was just not capable of pushing a wheelbarrow, that he must be found a softer job because he could no longer earn his living with his hands, then we should apply the principle on which pensions are paid. If the Hong Kong veteran is incapable of earning his living with his hands, as a farm labourer or even pushing a wheelbarrow, then the principle we have always followed is that if he is 50 per cent reduced in this ability he receives a 50 per cent disability pension. Whether or not he has a leg off, if you reasonably believe that the reason he is only 50 per cent capable of earning his living with his hands is a result of serving for four years in a prisoner of war camp in Hong Kong, then that is a legitimate war disability and I for one say he is entitled to our deepest consideration.
Dr. Crawford has done signal service in providing medical services to veterans under
D.V.A. Largely of his own volition and in his own time he has made a detailed study of this whole question. I have discussed the matter thoroughly with Dr. Crawford and found him to be a very fine man in his attitude to these people. Not only has he made a study of this question but he himself suffered as a prisoner of war and knows the physical hardships which these men went through from his own personal experiences. He is a giant of a man, but neither he nor anybody else would expect the average soldier to be able to rehabilitate himself and fit into society after the war in spite of the terrible experiences these men went through.
I would say that Dr. Crawford has made perhaps the most outstanding contribution to our information on this subject, but I believe he could do more if he was given more funds and had more help. Either he or some younger doctor could do a great deal more and look into these rather strange symptoms exhibited by a man who has been nearly starved to death or perhaps temporarily

The Hong Kong veterans as a group have no funds available to make such a study or they would be pleased to do so, I am sure. They also have no advocate to pursue the matter for them.
If I as an individual were fighting a pension case I could appeal it and have an advocate assist me with my case. These advocates are usually very experienced in the law, particularly in this type of subject. But to my knowledge, the Hong Kong veterans have no way of getting the services of an advocate to take their case and to make sure that they as a group will get proper consideration. This is rather unique. For example, if I had lost a leg I would have had no difficulty in getting my case attended to. But this group is rather unique in the experiences and problems they have. I suggest they have an across the board problem inasmuch as their physical ability to earn their living with their hands has been reduced as a result of four years of near starvation.
I would suggest to the minister, and through him to his department, that he might take into consideration the appointment of a member of the legal profession or a member of the justice department to make representations on behalf of these men to medical societies, and so on, so as to find out what has been done in this type of case. This sort of evidence is available. The French have made quite an extensive study of the problem of tropical diseases connected with malnutrition and its side effects. The United States has not done as much as one might expect in view of the fact that they had hundreds of thousands of men who served in the Pacific. Nevertheless they have done something, and I suggest that this small minority group- perhaps only 1,200 men are involved-is certainly worthy of our greatest consideration. I should not like to think that the matter of spending a few thousand dollars to make a proper survey would stand in the way. This survey should be made quickly; it is no good bringing in a report 15 years from now. These boys have been out of the prison camps now for 20 years and old age and their physical disabilities are coming upon them. I should like to see immediate attention paid to this question, and if a proper study were carried out and a competent legal officer were to tie things up for them, a recommendation acceptable not only to the department but to the house as a whole could soon be brought down.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief because I do not wish to delay the pas-20220-589
Supply-Veterans Affairs sage of these estimates, which have all been thoroughly investigated previously both by hon. members in the committee today as well as when they came before the veterans affairs committee. However, I should like to lend my support to some of the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Timmins, particularly in respect to granting extra allowances with respect to children of recipients of war veterans allowance. The hon. member made a very good point there and I should like to support it. I also wish to support generally the idea which has been expressed in this house many times today, as well as in the veterans affairs committee, namely that there be a general increase in war veterans allowances. The reasons for this are too well known to require any elaboration here. The increase in the cost of living would justify this support to the hilt.
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I also have a personal interest in the Hong Kong veterans group. You will recall that I introduced a private member's notice of motion in this house earlier in the year. I have been very gratified indeed with the sympathetic reaction this has aroused in the house and across the country. I intended to bring this point to the attention of the minister, and although the speaker immediately preceding me made reference to it, I should like to reiterate it for emphasis. I urge the minister, in respect of the investigation now taking place by the Canadian pension commission in relation to certain Hong Kong veterans, that it be completed at the earliest possible date, and that some time limit be fixed within which a report shall be presented.
Mr. Chairman, I shall close my remarks with those few words. Thank you.

Mr. Chairman, I am not a
member of the veterans affairs committee of the house, but I have given some attention to the proceedings of that committee in consideration of the estimates of the minister's department. I was interested to note that at the outset of those proceedings the minister informed my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, that he was glad he would not have to discuss the Columbia river treaty. I notice today that he may be having some difficulty in avoiding that subject matter altogether.
In looking at the proceedings of that committee, and in listening to the discussion that has taken place this afternoon, it seems quite obvious that the main focus of interest of
9304	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs hon. members of this house at the present time is perhaps more in relation to changes in the legislation, which the minister indicated to the committee he intended to bring forward at an early date, than in relation to some of the questions of administration within his department. Certainly my main purpose in rising in my place today is to indicate my own feeling that that is the most urgent question which lies before us as members of the house.
Mr. Chairman, I have noticed a considerable change in the general attitude of the membership of this house in consideration of veterans affairs questions, even during the comparatively short time I have been a member of parliament. As other members have indicated today, I think there is a general recognition on the part of all of us that the members who initiated what is commonly referred to as the veterans charter did lay some sound foundations in the field of veterans legislation. What we are really seeking is not a basic change in much of that legislation, but rather the kind of improvement which will meet the situation existing today.
Other members have made reference to the fact, as did the minister, that generally speaking, because of the inevitable passage of time, the veterans of Canada as a group today are of an older age group than when the veterans charter was established, and for that reason I think it is perhaps fair to say that the emphasis of our interest is turning more toward questions of pension arrangements, whether disability or war allowances, than toward those matters which were of great concern to the members of this house shortly after the end of the second world war, involving immediate questions of rehabilitation, educational opportunities, the setting up of the Veterans Land Act, and things of that sort.
When the minister appeared before the veterans affairs committee he was optimistic, as ministers very often are, that the proposals he is going to bring forward will meet with the general approval of this house. I hope that will be the case. Other members have mentioned some of the things they hope this legislation will accomplish in the way of increases in war veterans allowances and other pension payments. Before the minister introduces this legislation I suggest that he consider what needs to be accomplished in the light of at least two facts. The first is the fact that the government, of which he is a member, is proposing to introduce a Canada pension plan


which, under the terms as presently proposed, will not really become fully operative for a period of ten years from the time of its passage. The second fact is one to which I have already referred, that the age group to which veterans belong generally is getting older. In other words a great many of the veterans in Canada will not really benefit as a result of a Canada pension plan. It seems to me that the steps taken in relation to war veterans allowances and veterans disability pension arrangements should be taken with that fact in mind.
Involved with that question is the other question, which has been referred to by a number of members this afternoon, relating to the benefit of doubt clause-that is to say, whether certain disabilities requiring pension arrangements are wholly or partially attributable directly to war service.
The second point I should like to bring to the minister's attention arises out of a proposal contained in the Canada pension plan, and to which consideration should be given. That is the idea of incorporating into pension arrangements for veterans one of the key principles of the proposed Canada pension plan. I refer to the arrangement whereby the pension plan is to be geared to the cost of living index or the general level of earnings index. During the first few years I was a member of this house, any member who proposed that a pension plan should be geared to that principle was labelled as an economic screwball. I remember that very vividly. Nevertheless as I have pointed out on more than one occasion, the government of Canada is actually taking some steps to incorporate that principle into the Canada pension plan. Certainly if any group in Canada should receive the benefits of the application of that principle to a pension plan, it is the veterans group of this country.
I believe revision should be made to war veterans allowances arrangements and to pensions for veterans, so that all veterans who may have requirements because of disabilities, but who, because of their age group, will not benefit from the introduction of the Canada pension plan, will be eligible for suitable pension arrangements. I hope that will result from the changes the minister has indicated he is going to propose.
The member for Simcoe East made reference to recognition of the need for the milk: of human kindness. As a result of my experience in dealing with individuals in the-minister's department who look after the ad-

ministration of veterans affairs, I am of the opinion that while there may be some minor incidents which would indicate a certain lack of the milk of human kindness, basically the the question relating to the milk of human kindness is one which the members of this house must consider in relation to legislation. It is fair to say that 99.9 per cent of the problems I have encountered in respect of individual veterans situations arise really, not from administration, but from the kind of legislation we in this house have said these people must administer, and the regulations that have flowed from that legislation.
I suggest it is very much the responsibility of the government and members of the house to take the necessary steps to remedy situations of the kind that have been mentioned by my colleague from Timmins and other members of the house this afternoon. I could also give similar examples if I wished to take the time. I certainly wish the minister well in his endeavours to bring about the early introduction of the proposed legislative changes and I hope they will live up to the anticipations many of us have with regard to improvements in the situation of the veterans.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased today to have the opportunity to say a few words on the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. It is not my usual custom to congratulate the minister on his work because I feel it is not good to embarrass a minister in such a way. However, there are two points on which I will congratulate him. First, he has been appointed to a department which has always been staffed by dedicated men and women who give everything they possibly can to the cause of the veterans, and who do so willingly and without stint. He has also been appointed to a department with regard to which there is very seldom any real controversy or trouble in getting the estimates passed. Some of us at times may wish to say things that are aimed at being helpful to the department in the administration of veterans affairs, and this may take a little longer in discussing the minister's estimates than the minister might wish.
In making my remarks I know I am reiterating and repeating things that have been said by other members but I feel I should do so. I also want to point out to the committee that any changes in the acts found in the veterans charter are not the responsibility of the people who administer those acts but are the responsibility of the government of the moment and of parliament.
20220-589i
Supply-Veterans Affairs Therefore any changes that must be made are our responsibility. Any suggestions I may make will be made in that light.
I feel that the minister must take the advice contained in the recommendations of the standing committee on veterans affairs. Those recommendations are made by a committee composed of a goodly number of members of all parties in the house, and naturally they are made with the idea of helping those veterans who were not so fortunate as some of us who came back from the wars more or less in one piece.
In making my remarks I want to support particularly what the hon. member for Oka-nagan-Revelstoke, the hon. member for Sim-coe East and the other hon. members have said. I also want to remind the minister that all changes in veterans legislation should and must be discussed with the veterans organizations first before they are put into effect.
There are some special matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, the first being an increase in veterans pensions and war veterans allowances. In this day and age the recipients of war veterans allowances are not getting assistance adequate enough for them to live decently. The cost of living has increased and that situation affects veterans as well as all others. Most veterans have some other means of livelihood, but those who have nothing more than their pensions are entirely dependant on what they receive in this way, and their pensions should be increased whenever the cost of living rises or perhaps whenever civil servants are given a raise in pay. I know that would be fairly frequently, but what group of people is more deserving of having their means of livelihood increased than those veterans who were not so fortunate as most of us who were in the services?
Adequate veterans legislation is approved by practically everybody in Canada. There are between two and three million people who have a direct interest in veterans legislation and they are the greatest exponents of proper assistance. With regard to veterans pensions and war veterans allowance awards a great deal has been said about the benefit of the doubt. I realize quite well that the pension commission, the war veterans allowance board and the other boards concerned fulfil adequately on most occasions the spirit of the benefit of the doubt clause in veterans legislation. However, there are cases where it does seem that somebody has slipped up with regard to the benefit of the doubt clause, and it would appear to one on the outside that a
9306	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs little more consideration could have been given in some cases. Personally I have not brought too many cases to the attention of the Department of Veterans Affairs in which the benefit of the doubt clause has not been given full consideration. In fact, Mr. Chairman, the Department of Veterans Affairs is very good and, on the whole, I am satisfied with the treatment I have received on behalf of my veterans.
There is something, though, about veterans pensions which I feel should be given greater consideration. As I understand it, if a veteran receives less than a 50 per cent pension there is no continuing pension to the wife should the veteran die. I feel that more consideration should be given to the provision of assistance to the surviving partner in cases where veterans have been receiving less than a 50 per cent pension.
In so far as the war veterans allowance is concerned, I said that in many cases the amount authorized does not seem to be adequate to meet the needs of the veteran concerned. I believe it should be increased. I know there is a movement afoot in places suggesting that there be no means test in connection with war veterans allowance when an applicant is over 65 years of age. I make no recommendation in that respect, except that I would suggest to the minister he pay some attention to investigating the claims of people in this category.
The Veterans Land Act seems to be exceedingly well administered, and there is very little difficulty now with that. I am pleased to note that the Veterans Land Act is again operating as a unit and not as part of the Farm Credit Corporation.
I now come to my few remarks about veterans who were prisoners of war in the east, commonly referred to as the Hong Kong veterans. I know that the director of medical services is looking after these people. I know that he is torn by his loyalty to his fellow prisoners of war from Hong Kong, and I know that he has done everything possible to help them. However, there is a feeling amongst a great many of the Hong Kong prisoners of war that they are getting something less than they deserve. There is a feeling that they should be set aside as a special class, because of the extra privations that they were forced to undergo. I was fortunate. I was not a prisoner of war anywhere, so I do not really know exactly what the difficulties were. However, I do know these men went

through great hardship, and the majority of them feel that they were subjected to more severe treatment than prisoners in other theatres of war. I ask the minister therefore to do everything possible to see that these men get whatever consideration they deserve, over and above the consideration which the rest of the veterans receive. I have conferred with many of them and the complaints are the same throughout. They feel their treatment was much worse than that received by prisoners in other countries.
This item was discussed at length in the veterans affairs committee and a recommendation was made by that committee to the effect the veterans of Hong Kong should have their cases investigated.
The last time I spoke on the matter of veterans hospitals and the turning over of these hospitals to civilian control, I said that I thought until adequate facilities for domiciliary care could be provided there should be no question of turning over veterans hospitals to civilian organizations. I still feel this way. As I said, I believe the veterans receive more consideration in hospitals operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs than they would receive in hospitals operated by other organizations. I feel that until adequate care can be assured for the aging veterans who are not surgical cases, the hospitals must be retained within the control of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.
